claim: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the leading cause of dementia.
source: Alzheimer's disease (AD), the leading cause of dementia, could potentially be mitigated through early detection and interventions.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the scientific literature, supported by citation to Nandi et al., 2022 in the introduction.

claim: Abnormal biomarkers can appear years before symptoms arise in AD, a stage referred to as preclinical AD.
source: Abnormal biomarkers can appear years before symptoms arise, a stage referred to as preclinical AD (Sperling et al., 2011; Sperling et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sperling et al., 2011 and Sperling et al., 2014.

claim: Cognitive decline has been reported in a wide range of domains as early as a decade before dementia.
source: Cognitive decline has been reported in a wide range of domains, including memory, language, visuospatial function, and executive function, leading to behavioral change as early as a decade before dementia (Amieva et al., 2008; Knopman et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Amieva et al., 2008 and Knopman et al., 2021.

claim: Memory impairment is the predominant first symptom of AD.
source: Memory impairment is the predominant first symptom of AD (Barnes et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barnes et al., 2015.

claim: The AppNL-G-F knock-in AD mouse model carries the Swedish KM670/671 NL, Iberian I716F, and Arctic E693G mutations on the gene of amyloid-β precursor protein (APP).
source: This model of mice carries the Swedish KM670/671 NL, Iberian I716F, and Arctic E693G mutations on the gene of amyloid-β precursor protein (APP) and displays Aβ plaque accumulation and neuroinflammation across age, reproducing neuropathological change in preclinical AD without artifacts caused by APP overexpression (Saito et al., 2014; Sasaguri et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Saito et al., 2014 and Sasaguri et al., 2017.

claim: The AppNL-G-F mouse model displays Aβ plaque accumulation and neuroinflammation across age.
source: This model of mice carries the Swedish KM670/671 NL, Iberian I716F, and Arctic E693G mutations on the gene of amyloid-β precursor protein (APP) and displays Aβ plaque accumulation and neuroinflammation across age, reproducing neuropathological change in preclinical AD without artifacts caused by APP overexpression (Saito et al., 2014; Sasaguri et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Saito et al., 2014 and Sasaguri et al., 2017.

claim: The AppNL-G-F mouse model reproduces neuropathological change in preclinical AD without artifacts caused by APP overexpression.
source: This model of mice carries the Swedish KM670/671 NL, Iberian I716F, and Arctic E693G mutations on the gene of amyloid-β precursor protein (APP) and displays Aβ plaque accumulation and neuroinflammation across age, reproducing neuropathological change in preclinical AD without artifacts caused by APP overexpression (Saito et al., 2014; Sasaguri et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Saito et al., 2014 and Sasaguri et al., 2017.

claim: AppNL-G-F mice exhibited a lower extent of reinstatement of fear memory.
source: The results showed that AppNL-G-F mice exhibited a lower extent of reinstatement of fear memory.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the study, specifically shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The deficit in the AppNL-G-F mice would be due to their internal states being biased toward overgeneralization or overdifferentiation of their observations.
source: Computational modeling revealed that the deficit in the AppNL-G-F mice would be due to their internal states being biased toward overgeneralization or overdifferentiation of their observations, and consequently, the competing memories were not retained.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling analysis of the experimental data, as shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: AppNL-G-F mice failed to retain competing memories because of the misclassification of observation into memories.
source: We concluded that the altered internal states of AppNL-G-F mice illustrated their misclassification in the memory modification process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational modeling and behavioral data presented in the study.

claim: AppNL-G-F mice, given spatial cues, failed to infer coexisting memories for two goal locations during the trial in the reversal Barnes maze task.
source: Following reversal learning, AppNL-G-F mice, given spatial cues, failed to infer coexisting memories for two goal locations during the trial.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the reversal Barnes maze task, as shown in Figure 6.

claim: The latent cause model proposed by Gershman et al., 2017b provides a normative account of memory modification phenomena in Pavlovian fear conditioning.
source: Previously, Gershman et al., 2017b proposed the latent cause model, which provides a normative account of memory modification phenomena in Pavlovian fear conditioning.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gershman et al., 2017b.

claim: In the latent cause model, an agent infers a latent cause as a source of the co-occurrence of events in the environment.
source: The latent cause model proposed by Gershman et al., 2010 is an internal model such that an agent infers a latent cause as a source of the co-occurrence of events in the environment.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gershman et al., 2010.

claim: In the latent cause model, stimuli and outcome at time t are generated at an associative strength from k-th latent cause.
source: In the latent cause model, an agent learning an association between a conditioned stimulus (CS) and an unconditioned stimulus (US) has an internal model such that stimuli x (i.e., d-dimensional vector involving the CS or context) and outcome r (i.e., US) at time t are generated at an associative strength w (i.e., d-dimensional vector) from k-th latent cause ztk of total K latent causes by a likelihood p(x|ztk) and p(r|ztk), respectively (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the mathematical formulation of the latent cause model, referencing Figure 1A.

claim: The prior of latent causes follows the Chinese restaurant process.
source: The prior of z follows the Chinese restaurant process
evidence: This is a mathematical property of the latent cause model as described in the text.

claim: Higher concentration parameter α biases the agent to infer a new latent cause given an observation (i.e. differentiation) rather than to infer an old one (i.e., generalization).
source: A new latent cause is inferred at a probability governed by the concentration parameter α. Higher α or lower likelihood of the current observation biases the agent to infer a new latent cause given an observation (i.e. differentiation) rather than to infer an old one (i.e., generalization) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the effect of the concentration parameter α in the latent cause model, referencing Figure 1B.

claim: Reinstatement occurs when agents who have learned and then extinguished an association between a CS and a US exhibit CR again after being exposed to the US alone following the extinction.
source: Reinstatement occurs when agents who have learned and then extinguished an association between a CS and a US exhibit CR again after being exposed to the US alone following the extinction.
evidence: This is a definition of reinstatement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: 6- and 12-month-old AppNL-G-F knock-in AD model mice and age-matched control mice underwent memory modification learning consisting of classical fear conditioning, extinction, and reinstatement.
source: The 6- and 12-month-old AppNL-G-F knock-in AD model mice and the age-matched control mice underwent memory modification learning, which consisted of classical fear conditioning, extinction, and reinstatement.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: In the acquisition phase of fear conditioning, the freezing rate gradually increased with the number of CS-US pairings.
source: In the acquisition phase of fear conditioning, the freezing rate gradually increased with the number of CS-US pairings (Figure 2B, leftmost red panel).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: AppNL-G-F mice showed a higher freezing rate than control mice in test 1 phase.
source: In the test 1 phase, 24 hr after the acquisition, a significant genotype effect was observed in freezing rates during CS presentation [F(1,95) = 9.679, p = 0.002], where the AppNL-G-F mice showed a higher freezing rate than in the control (Figure 2C and Supplementary file 1b)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Both control and AppNL-G-F mice showed a gradually decreased freezing rate in the extinction phase.
source: As the increasing trials of CS alone presented, both groups showed a gradually decreased freezing rate in the extinction phase (Figure 2B, blue panel).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In test 2 phase, 12-month-old mice showed a higher freezing rate than 6-month-old mice.
source: In the test 2 phase, 24 hr after the last trial of the extinction, there was a significant age effect in freezing rates during CS presentation [F(1,95) = 4.698, p = 0.033], where 12-month-old mice showed a higher freezing rate than in the 6-month-old mice (Figure 2D and Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In test 3 phase, no significant genotype or age effect was detected in freezing rate.
source: In the test 3 phase, 24 hr after given an unsignaled shock, mice showed an elevated freezing rate, and no significant genotype or age effect was detected (Figure 2B and E and Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2B and E.

claim: The DIs between test 2 and test 1 were significantly lower than 0.5 in all groups.
source: The results showed that the DIs between test 2 and test 1 were significantly lower than 0.5 in all groups (Figure 2F and Supplementary file 1c), indicating the successful establishment of extinction memory.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: AppNL-G-F mice showed lower DI values between test 2 and test 1 compared to control mice.
source: The genotype effect was detected [F(1,95) = 5.013, p = 0.027] (Figure 2F and Supplementary file 1d), where AppNL-G-F mice showed lower values due to higher freezing in the test 1 phase.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The DIs between test 3 and 2 phases in four groups were significantly higher than 0.5.
source: The DIs between the test 3 and 2 phases in four groups were significantly higher than 0.5, indicating that the reinstatement was successfully induced after the unsignaled shock (Figure 2G and Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Six-month-old mice showed higher DIs between test 3 and test 2 compared to 12-month-old mice.
source: Six-month-old mice showed higher DIs, as a significant age effect was detected [F(1,95) = 7.480, p = 0.007] (Figure 2G and Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The DIs between test 3 and 1 phases did not deviate from 0.5 for both 6- and 12-month-old control mice.
source: The DIs between the test 3 and 1 phases did not deviate from 0.5 for both 6- and 12-month-old control mice, suggesting that they displayed comparable freezing rates in tests 1 and 3 (Figure 2H and Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The DIs between test 3 and 1 phases were significantly lower than 0.5 in 6-month-old AppNL-G-F mice.
source: In contrast, the DIs between test 3 and 1 phases were significantly lower than 0.5 in 6-month-old AppNL-G-F mice [t(24) = –3.245, p = 0.003] and 12-month-old AppNL-G-F mice [t(24) = –6.165, p < 0.001] (Figure 2H and Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The DIs between test 3 and 1 phases were significantly lower than 0.5 in 12-month-old AppNL-G-F mice.
source: In contrast, the DIs between test 3 and 1 phases were significantly lower than 0.5 in 6-month-old AppNL-G-F mice [t(24) = –3.245, p = 0.003] and 12-month-old AppNL-G-F mice [t(24) = –6.165, p < 0.001] (Figure 2H and Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: A significant genotype effect was detected in DI between test 3 and test 1, indicating AppNL-G-F mice exhibited a lower extent of reinstatement.
source: Moreover, a significant genotype effect was detected [F(1,95) = 15.393, p < 0.001] (Figure 2H and Supplementary file 1d), indicating AppNL-G-F mice exhibited a lower extent of reinstatement.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: AppNL-G-F mice had significantly lower concentration parameter α than control mice at 12 months of age.
source: AppNL-G-F mice had significantly lower α (Mann-Whitney U = 100, p = 0.002) and lower σx2 (Mann-Whitney U = 88.5, p = 0.008) than control mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the computational modeling analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: AppNL-G-F mice had significantly lower σx2 than control mice at 12 months of age.
source: AppNL-G-F mice had significantly lower α (Mann-Whitney U = 100, p = 0.002) and lower σx2 (Mann-Whitney U = 88.5, p = 0.008) than control mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the computational modeling analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: α and σx2 were significantly correlated with each other in 12-month-old mice.
source: α and σx2 were significantly correlated each other (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the computational modeling analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both α and σx2 were positively correlated with the DI between test 3 and test 1 in 12-month-old mice.
source: Both were also positively correlated with the DI (Figure 4B), and the trend was preserved after adjusting for the genotype effect (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the computational modeling analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The number of latent causes initially inferred at the acquisition phase was significantly lower in 12-month-old AppNL-G-F mice.
source: Indeed, the number of latent causes initially inferred at the acquisition phase was significantly lower in AppNL-G-F mice, where most of them inferred two latent causes, and more than half of the control mice inferred three latent causes (Figure 4C and Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the computational modeling analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The posterior probabilities of acquisition latent causes in test 1 were significantly higher in 12-month-old AppNL-G-F mice than in control mice.
source: Furthermore, when they initially observed the CS in the absence of the US in test 1, the posterior probabilities of acquisition latent causes in test 1 were significantly higher in the AppNL-G-F mice than in the control mice, leading to the higher CRs in test 1 in the simulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), consistent with the observed CR (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The number of latent causes acquired at the extinction phase was comparable between 12-month-old control and AppNL-G-F mice.
source: Repeated observation of the CS alone during the extinction would sufficiently increase the likelihood of stimuli given the latent causes inferred during the extinction in both AppNL-G-F and control mice. This attenuates the need to infer new latent causes and the number of latent causes acquired at the extinction phase was comparable between groups (Figure 4D and Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The number of latent causes acquired after the extinction was greater in 12-month-old AppNL-G-F mice than in control mice.
source: As a result, the number of latent causes acquired after the extinction (i.e., the unsignaled shock and test 3) as well as the sum of posterior probabilities of them were greater in AppNL-G-F mice than those in the control mice, despite that the mice received either the US or the CS alone that were the same with those they observed so far (Figure 4E and Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: AppNL-G-F mice had significantly lower α than control mice at 6 months of age.
source: We found that AppNL-G-F mice had significantly lower α (Mann-Whitney U = 38, p = 0.012), and it was significantly correlated with DI (Figure 5A and B and Supplementary file 1j, k).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the computational modeling analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: α was significantly correlated with DI in 6-month-old mice.
source: We found that AppNL-G-F mice had significantly lower α (Mann-Whitney U = 38, p = 0.012), and it was significantly correlated with DI (Figure 5A and B and Supplementary file 1j, k).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the computational modeling analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: σx2 was significantly correlated with DI in 6-month-old mice.
source: The σx2 was comparable between control and AppNL-G-F mice, but its significant correlation with DI was found (Figure 5A and B and Supplementary file 1j, k).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the computational modeling analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The hyperparameter θ was significantly higher in 6-month-old AppNL-G-F mice than in control mice.
source: The hyperparameter θ, a threshold to emit CR for stimulus inputs, was significantly higher in AppNL-G-F mice than in control mice.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the computational modeling analysis.

claim: AppNL-G-F and control mice exhibited similar learning curves in the initial training phase of the Barnes maze regardless of age.
source: The AppNL-G-F and control mice exhibited similar learning curves in the initial training phase regardless of age (Figure 6—figure supplements 1A and 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 1A and 3A.

claim: The usage of confirmatory strategy was significantly higher in 12-month-old control mice during the reversal training phase.
source: The usage of confirmatory strategy, such that mice selectively explored the first and the second target hole was significantly higher in the control mice during the reversal training phase, especially in the 12-month-old (Figure 6B and F).
evidence: This is a finding from the strategy analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: AppNL-G-F mice primarily took the perimeter search strategy during reversal training.
source: In contrast, the AppNL-G-F mice primarily took the perimeter search strategy such that mice explored the target hole in a 'brute-force' manner (Figure 6B and F), consistent with deficits in navigation ability found in preclinical AD patients (Allison et al., 2016; Coughlan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the strategy analysis shown in Figure 6B and F, with supporting citations.

claim: AppNL-G-F mice spent significantly less time around the target hole than control mice in probe test 1.
source: Consequently, AppNL-G-F mice spent significantly less time around the target hole than control mice did in the probe test 1, as a significant interaction between genotype and holes [F(11, 374) = 4.22, p < 0.001] was detected (Figure 6C and Supplementary file 1o).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The DI for the second target hole was significantly higher than 0.5 in 12-month-old control mice.
source: The DI for the second target hole was significantly higher than 0.5 in control mice, indicating that the mice successfully modified the spatial memories from probe test 1 to probe test 2 at a discriminable level (Figure 6E and Supplementary file 1p).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The DI for the second target hole in 12-month-old AppNL-G-F mice was comparable to 0.5 and significantly lower than that of control mice.
source: On the contrary, the DI in AppNL-G-F mice was comparable to 0.5 and significantly lower than that of control mice, indicating that their spatial memory for the second target hole was not modified after the reversal learning (Figure 6E and Supplementary file 1p).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The widespread of Aβ accumulation was confirmed in AppNL-G-F mice.
source: The widespread of Aβ accumulation was confirmed in this study, and results were provided in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This is confirmed by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Aβ plaque area was significantly higher in 12-month-old AppNL-G-F mice compared to 6-month-old AppNL-G-F mice in anterior coronal sections.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Aβ plaque area was significantly higher in 12-month-old AppNL-G-F mice compared to 6-month-old AppNL-G-F mice in posterior coronal sections.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The amygdala, the hippocampus, and the medial prefrontal cortex are critical in regulating fear memory and its extinction.
source: It is well known that the amygdala, the hippocampus, and the medial prefrontal cortex are critical in regulating fear memory and its extinction (Maren et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maren et al., 2013.

claim: The ventral tegmental area (VTA) plays a modulatory role with its wide projection to the amygdala, hippocampus, and medial prefrontal cortex.
source: In addition, the ventral tegmental area (VTA) plays a modulatory role with its wide projection to these brain regions (Beier et al., 2015; Cai and Tong, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Beier et al., 2015 and Cai and Tong, 2022.

claim: Inhibition of dopaminergic signal from VTA to the infralimbic cortex during unsignaled shock reduced the reinstatement of fear memory in mice.
source: Indeed, previous studies have shown that the inhibition of dopaminergic signal from VTA to the infralimbic cortex (Hitora-Imamura et al., 2015) or inhibition of glutamatergic signal from VTA to the dorsal hippocampus (Han et al., 2020) during unsignaled shock reduced the reinstatement of fear memory in mice.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hitora-Imamura et al., 2015.

claim: Inhibition of glutamatergic signal from VTA to the dorsal hippocampus during unsignaled shock reduced the reinstatement of fear memory in mice.
source: Indeed, previous studies have shown that the inhibition of dopaminergic signal from VTA to the infralimbic cortex (Hitora-Imamura et al., 2015) or inhibition of glutamatergic signal from VTA to the dorsal hippocampus (Han et al., 2020) during unsignaled shock reduced the reinstatement of fear memory in mice.
evidence: Supported by citation to Han et al., 2020.

claim: Prediction error in classical or operant conditioning learning is computed in the VTA.
source: It is well established that prediction error in classical or operant conditioning learning is computed in the VTA (Lerner et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lerner et al., 2021.

claim: The prediction error is signaled from the VTA to the hippocampal CA1 via the dopaminergic projections.
source: The prediction error is signaled from the VTA to the hippocampal CA1 via the dopaminergic projections, while the VTA receives a feedback signal from the CA1 (Lisman and Grace, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lisman and Grace, 2005.

claim: The pattern separation and completion were implemented in the dentate gyrus (DG) and the CA3 in the hippocampus, respectively.
source: The pattern separation and completion were implemented in the dentate gyrus (DG) and the CA3 in the hippocampus, respectively (Neunuebel and Knierim, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Neunuebel and Knierim, 2014.

claim: The dysfunction in the VTA-hippocampus circuit has long been implicated in memory problems in aging and AD.
source: The dysfunction in this circuit has long been implicated in memory problems in aging and AD (Palmer and Good, 2011; Wilson et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Palmer and Good, 2011 and Wilson et al., 2006.

claim: AppNL-G-F mice showed lower neuronal firing rates in the CA1 region.
source: Different lines of evidence suggest that hippocampus functions were affected in AppNL-G-F mice, including lower neuronal firing rates in the CA1 region (Inayat et al., 2023)
evidence: Supported by citation to Inayat et al., 2023.

claim: AppNL-G-F mice showed degradation of gamma oscillation power in the CA3 region.
source: Different lines of evidence suggest that hippocampus functions were affected in AppNL-G-F mice, including lower neuronal firing rates in the CA1 region (Inayat et al., 2023), degradation of gamma oscillation power in the CA3 region (Arroyo-García et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to Arroyo-García et al., 2021.

claim: AppNL-G-F mice showed disrupted place cell remapping in CA1 region.
source: Different lines of evidence suggest that hippocampus functions were affected in AppNL-G-F mice, including lower neuronal firing rates in the CA1 region (Inayat et al., 2023), degradation of gamma oscillation power in the CA3 region (Arroyo-García et al., 2021), and disrupted place cell remapping in CA1 region (Jun et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jun et al., 2020.

claim: Neurodegeneration in the VTA occurred at an early age in Tg2576 mice and consequent dysfunction was correlated with impairments in the hippocampus.
source: While VTA dysfunction was not reported in AppNL-G-F mice, studies using Tg2576 mice, which overexpress mutated APP, have shown that neurodegeneration in the VTA occurred at an early age and consequent dysfunction was correlated with impairments in the hippocampus (Nobili et al., 2017; Spoleti et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nobili et al., 2017 and Spoleti et al., 2024.

claim: The latent cause model explains the reinstatement of fear memory with the changes of agent's internal state.
source: The latent cause model explains the reinstatement of fear memory with the changes of agent's internal state as follows.
evidence: This is an explanation of how the latent cause model works, based on the model's theoretical framework.

claim: In the latent cause model, the agent solves two computational problems during Pavlovian fear conditioning learning: computing the posterior probability of each latent cause and computing the associative weight of each latent cause.
source: According to the latent cause model, the agent solves two computational problems during Pavlovian fear conditioning learning. One is to compute the posterior probability of each latent cause given its associative weight between stimuli x and shock r with a history of observations, and the other is to compute the associative weight of each latent cause given its posterior.
evidence: This describes the computational framework of the latent cause model.

claim: Both computations in the latent cause model are achieved through the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm.
source: Both computations are achieved through the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm, as the former and the latter computation correspond to E-step and M-step, respectively.
evidence: This describes the computational implementation of the latent cause model.

claim: The weight in the latent cause model is updated based on the Rescorla-Wagner rule.
source: The weight is updated based on the Rescorla-Wagner rule (Rescorla and Wagner, 1972) to minimize the prediction error between observed and predicted shock.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rescorla and Wagner, 1972.

claim: The latent cause model was adapted to model the memory modification process in the Pavlovian fear conditioning paradigm in rodents and humans.
source: It was later adapted to model the memory modification process, a problem to infer previously acquired latent causes or a novel latent cause for every observation in the Pavlovian fear conditioning paradigm in rodents and humans (Gershman et al., 2017b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gershman et al., 2017b.

claim: The likelihood that α > 0 in human participants correlates with the degree of their spontaneous recovery.
source: As demonstrated in Gershman and Hartley, 2015, the likelihood that α > 0 in human participants correlates with the degree of their spontaneous recovery, that is, a return of the CR after a long hiatus following an extinction procedure.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gershman and Hartley, 2015.

claim: The latent cause model explains maladaptive decision-making in post-traumatic stress disorder patients as a perseverated inference of previously acquired latent causes.
source: Furthermore, a recent study has shown that the latent cause model explains maladaptive decision-making in post-traumatic stress disorder patients as a perseverated inference of previously acquired latent causes even under situations where they should infer novel latent causes (Norbury et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Norbury et al., 2022.

claim: Severe post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) patients were biased to infer old memories rather than to acquire new memories for novel observations, as they have a lower concentration parameter α.
source: For instance, Norbury et al., 2022 simulated a memory modification process in severe post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) patients by the latent cause model and found that they were biased to infer old memories rather than to acquire new memories for novel observations, as they have a lower concentration parameter α.
evidence: Supported by citation to Norbury et al., 2022.

claim: AppNL-G-F mice displayed Aβ plaque accumulation from 4 months old.
source: According to previous studies, the AppNL-G-F mice displayed an age-dependent Aβ deposition from 4 months old and memory impairments could be detected at 6 months of age (Masuda et al., 2016; Saito et al., 2014; Sakakibara et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Masuda et al., 2016, Saito et al., 2014, and Sakakibara et al., 2018.

claim: Memory impairments could be detected at 6 months of age in AppNL-G-F mice.
source: According to previous studies, the AppNL-G-F mice displayed an age-dependent Aβ deposition from 4 months old and memory impairments could be detected at 6 months of age (Masuda et al., 2016; Saito et al., 2014; Sakakibara et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Masuda et al., 2016, Saito et al., 2014, and Sakakibara et al., 2018.

claim: The CS freezing rate was significantly higher than the preCS freezing rate in all groups in test 3.
source: When we compared the preCS freezing rate (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E) and the CS freezing rate (Figure 2E) in test 3 within group by the paired samples t-tests, the CS freezing rate was significantly higher than the preCS freezing rate in all groups: 6-month-old control, t(23) = –6.344, p < 0.001, d = –1.295; 6-month-old AppNL-G-F, t(24) = –4.679, p < 0.001, d = –0.936; 12-month-old control, t(23) = –4.512, p < 0.001, d = –0.921; 12-month-old AppNL-G-F, t(24) = –2.408, p = 0.024, d = –0.482.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data comparing preCS and CS freezing rates.

claim: Reinstatement was not solely explained by the CR for context, but also reactivation acquisition memory.
source: Although the associative strength between the context and the US would be increased by the unsignaled shock, these results suggest that reinstatement was not solely explained by the CR for context, but also reactivation acquisition memory.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of preCS and CS freezing rates in test 3.

claim: Two latent causes were generated in the acquisition phase with increasing associative weight in the 6-month-old group.
source: In the 6-month-old group, two latent causes (z1 and z2) were generated in the acquisition phase with increasing associative weight (rows 2–4 in Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is an observation from the computational modeling results shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: During the extinction phase in 6-month-old mice, the same latent causes were inferred, and the corresponding associative weights declined.
source: During the extinction phase, the same latent causes were inferred, and the corresponding associative weights declined, indicating the devaluation of previously acquired fear memory (rows 2–4 in Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is an observation from the computational modeling results shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The wcs in w2 in 6-month-old control mice remained at a higher value compared to that in AppNL-G-F mice during extinction.
source: Notably, the wcs in w2 in control mice remained at a higher value compared to that in AppNL-G-F mice.
evidence: This is an observation from the computational modeling results shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: New latent causes were inferred during the extinction phase in the 12-month-old group.

claim: At trial 35 given an unsignaled shock, 12-month-old control mice inferred the latent causes acquired in the extinction phase so that their weights were updated.

evidence: This is an observation from the computational modeling results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: At trial 35 given an unsignaled shock, there was virtually no update of weights in 12-month-old AppNL-G-F mice.
source: In contrast, there was virtually no update of weights in AppNL-G-F mice (row 4 in Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an observation from the computational modeling results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: At trial 36 (test 3 phase), the elevated CR in 12-month-old control mice was attributed to a successful update of associative weight after the unsignaled shock.
source: At trial 36 (test 3 phase), the elevated CR in control mice was attributed to a successful update of associative weight after the unsignaled shock (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is an inference from the computational modeling results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: At trial 36 (test 3 phase), the CR in 12-month-old AppNL-G-F mice did not increase due to a redundant latent cause which was newly inferred and reduced the posterior probability of latent causes having higher associative weight.

claim: The DIs in the simulated CRs in each group well replicated those in the observed CRs, except that the DI between test 3 and test 1 in the 6-month-old AppNL-G-F mice did not significantly deviate from 0.5 in simulated results.

Figure 2F–H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).

claim: In test 3, the residual was significantly higher in the 12-month-old control mice than AppNL-G-F mice, indicating the model underestimated the reinstatement in the control mice.

claim: Lower α would bias AppNL-G-F mice toward overgeneralization, as they favor inferring a small number of latent causes when facing the same cue.
source: Lower α and lower σx2 would bias AppNL-G-F mice toward overgeneralization, as they favor inferring a small number of latent causes when facing the same cue.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the latent cause model and the estimated parameters.

evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the latent cause model and the estimated parameters.

claim: The associative weights in the extinction latent causes were increased by the unsignaled shock in the 12-month-old control mice.
source: Since the update of the associative weight of each latent cause is modulated by both prediction error and posterior probability of the latent cause, the associative weights in the extinction latent causes were increased by the unsignaled shock in the control mice (Figures 3C and 4G and Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: This is an observation from the computational modeling results shown in Figures 3C and 4G.

claim: In 12-month-old AppNL-G-F mice, they inferred new latent causes with low associative weight after the extinction, which decreased the posterior probabilities of other latent causes and impeded update of their weight.
source: In AppNL-G-F mice, however, they inferred new latent causes with low associative weight after the extinction (Figure 4E and H and Supplementary file 1i), which decreased the posterior probabilities of other latent causes and impeded update of their weight (Figures 3D and 4G).
evidence: This is an observation from the computational modeling results shown in Figures 3D, 4E, 4G, and 4H.

claim: The α and σx2 would differentiate the internal state and thereby behavioral phenotypes between 12-month-old AppNL-G-F and control mice.
source: These results suggest that the α and σx2 would differentiate the internal state and thereby behavioral phenotypes between AppNL-G-F and control mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational modeling analysis.

claim: In the Chinese restaurant process, the probability that a new latent cause is inferred decreases with trials, preventing that too many latent causes are inferred.
source: In the Chinese restaurant process, the probability that a new latent cause is inferred decreases with trials, preventing that too many latent causes are inferred (Gershman and Blei, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gershman and Blei, 2012.

claim: The overgeneralization by lower α was less effective than the overdifferentiation by lower σx2 in test 3 in 12-month-old AppNL-G-F mice.

evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the Chinese restaurant process and the computational modeling results.

claim: The λ was comparable between 6-month-old control and AppNL-G-F mice.

claim: The effect of higher θ was subtle when the expected US was far from its value in 6-month-old mice.

evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the latent cause model and the estimated parameters.

claim: AppNL-G-F mice did not find a significant spatial learning deficit up to 10 months old by using the Morris water maze.
source: These data align with previous studies that did not find a significant spatial learning deficit in AppNL-G-F mice up to 10 months old by using the Morris water maze, a common spatial learning task relevant to the Barnes maze (Latif-Hernandez et al., 2019; Saifullah et al., 2020; Whyte et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Latif-Hernandez et al., 2019, Saifullah et al., 2020, and Whyte et al., 2018.

claim: AppNL-G-F mice displayed behavioral flexibility as control mice did in the reversal training based on conventional analysis.
source: During the reversal training, AppNL-G-F mice displayed behavioral flexibility as control mice did based on the conventional analysis (Figure 6—figure supplements 2B and 3B), similar to findings in Sakakibara et al., 2018.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 2B and 3B, with supporting citation.

claim: The control mice solved the Barnes maze task by inferring the two competing spatial memories representing the two possible target holes.
source: These results suggest that the control mice solved the task by inferring the two competing spatial memories representing the two possible target holes, whereas the AppNL-G-F mice solved the task not relying on selective spatial memories but the perimeter strategy, while both mice were given the same spatial cues.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the strategy analysis and behavioral data.

claim: The AppNL-G-F mice solved the Barnes maze task not relying on selective spatial memories but the perimeter strategy.
source: These results suggest that the control mice solved the task by inferring the two competing spatial memories representing the two possible target holes, whereas the AppNL-G-F mice solved the task not relying on selective spatial memories but the perimeter strategy, while both mice were given the same spatial cues.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the strategy analysis and behavioral data.

claim: No significant correlations were detected between DIs in the reinstatement and the Barnes maze experiment.
source: Although both DIs in the reinstatement (Figure 2H) and the Barnes maze experiment (Figure 6E and I) suggest that inferred memories in each time point would diverge between the AppNL-G-F mice and the control mice, no significant correlations were detected (12-month-old group: Spearman's correlation coefficient = 0.062, p = 0.738, N = 32; 6-month-old group: Spearman's correlation coefficient = –0.029, p = 0.862, N = 39)
evidence: This is a statistical finding comparing DIs across different behavioral tasks.

claim: The lack of correlation between DIs in reinstatement and Barnes maze is potentially due to differential effects of Aβ accumulation on associative and instrumental learning.
source: no significant correlations were detected (12-month-old group: Spearman's correlation coefficient = 0.062, p = 0.738, N = 32; 6-month-old group: Spearman's correlation coefficient = –0.029, p = 0.862, N = 39), potentially due to differential effects of Aβ accumulation on associative and instrumental learning.
evidence: This is speculation about the reason for the lack of correlation.

claim: Identifying the earliest manifestation of cognitive decline is critical for intervention in AD.
source: Identifying the earliest manifestation of cognitive decline is critical for intervention.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of early detection in AD.

evidence: Supported by citation to Sutter et al., 2024.

claim: Learning rate in associative learning did not differ between amnestic MCI and AD patients and healthy controls.
source: To our knowledge, only a few studies tried to estimate internal states in amnestic MCI and AD patients and reported that a certain retention rate underlying motor learning (Sutter et al., 2024), but not learning rate in associative learning (Wessa et al., 2016) differed from healthy controls.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wessa et al., 2016.

source: Assuming an internal model would broaden and deepen interpretations of various cognitive deficits in terms of common computational account (Kocagoncu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kocagoncu et al., 2021.

source: In line with this, our perspective is that states of an internal model would be one candidate of factors to generate a wide variety of behavioral phenotypes in AD, and hence probing the internal state would contribute not only to detecting early signs of AD but also to multidimensionally evaluating how the disease gets worse and how early intervention works.

source: These results were the first to report the deficits in the reinstatement in the AppNL-G-F mice, suggesting that Aβ accumulation induces the defect in the memory modification process after the extinction.

Both overgeneralization and overdifferentiation could explain the lower exploration time of the target hole in the AppNL-G-F mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the latent cause framework applied to the Barnes maze results.

claim: The latent cause model was built on the fear conditioning paradigm and does not explicitly assume the contribution of other cognitive functions such as attention or working memory.
source: As the latent cause model was built on the fear conditioning paradigm and does not explicitly assume the contribution of other cognitive functions such as attention or working memory, this study provides no direct evidence as to which model parameters are in conjunction with the behavioral outcomes in the reversal Barnes maze and which parameters involve other the cognitive functions that are presumably affected by AD pathology (Finke et al., 2013; Kirova et al., 2015; Malhotra, 2019).
evidence: This is a limitation of the latent cause model as applied in this study.

claim: This study provides no direct evidence as to which model parameters are in conjunction with the behavioral outcomes in the reversal Barnes maze.

claim: Further studies would be required to integrate computational models encompassing different cognitive functions.
source: To evaluate them, further studies would be required to integrate computational models encompassing different cognitive functions, such as multiple successor representations (Madarasz and Behrens, 2019) or hidden state inference (Sanders et al., 2020) for spatial learning, upon more fundamental principles, such as the predictive coding in a hierarchical neural network (Kocagoncu et al., 2021).
